current_text.html: The censures, which may be inflicted by church courts, are admonition, suspension from the Sacraments, excommunication, suspension from office, and deposition from office. The censures of admonition or definite suspension from office shall be administered to an accused who, upon conviction, satisfies the court as to his repentance and makes such restitution as is appropriate. Such censure concludes the judicial process. The censures of indefinite suspension or excommunication shall be administered to an accused who, upon conviction, remains impenitent.

metadata.synopsis: An elder appealed Presbytery’s elevation, without additional process, of suspensions from office and the Sacraments to deposition and excommunication. The SJC granted the appeal, reversed in whole, and remanded, restoring the prior suspensions. Elevation required a hearing on incorrigibility and contumacy—with a charge, evidence, plea, and defense—but not a full de novo trial; disagreement with the original verdict alone was insufficient. The SJC left unresolved deposition from office when excommunication is absent.

occurrences.excerpt: …case, given that the censure, once delivered, concludes the judicial process (BCO 30-1)."

metadata.synopsis: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

metadata.synopsis: Herron and others challenged Presbytery’s decision to proceed to trial after a BCO 31-2 finding, his administrative suspension, denial of access to Presbytery records and meetings, and a public statement. The SJC sustained only the access issue: suspension from official functions did not remove his membership rights, though it did not entitle him to every investigative-committee document. Finding no clear error on the other issues, it ordered trial to proceed, temporarily stayed censure decisions, and postponed related complaints through trial and any appeal.

metadata.synopsis: Teaching elders challenged Korean Central Presbytery’s summary censure of a minister before an indictment was prepared. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s action because discipline preceded particular charges and a specific confession, and because an independent church lacked authority to impose PCA censure. It declared the underlying matter moot because the alleged event was twenty-one years old and the victim would not cooperate, ending the proceeding without remand. The ruling addressed neither the allegations’ merits nor all old charges categorically.

topics: express vs. implied will of session
metadata.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

relationships.title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

relationships.title: Dodson et al. v. Ohio Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

relationships.title: Fozard v. North Texas Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: At issue was whether North Texas Presbytery wrongly denied a complaint challenging Fort Worth Presbyterian Church’s “Special Case Felons” integration policy as contrary to Scripture. The SJC denied the complaint, holding that the complainant did not show the Session violated Scripture or the Constitution and that BCO 39-3.3 required deference absent clear error, leaving the lower-court actions in effect. The decision, adopted 20-1, expressly did not endorse the Respondents’ Preliminary Principles arguments; a concurrence disclaimed approval of the policy, and one member dissented.

relationships.title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

relationships.title: Bumgarner v. Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley

metadata.synopsis: A claimant sought BCO 40-5 review of Presbytery’s handling of his earlier judicial case, alleging grossly unconstitutional proceedings and delinquency in failing to investigate his 2012 deposition. The SJC found the application administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order because BCO 40-3 excludes judicial-case proceedings from review and control when notice of appeal or complaint has been given, and he had withdrawn his 2012 complaint acknowledging it could not be resubmitted. It dismissed under OMSJC 9.2(d). The concurrence added that BCO 40 cannot refile a withdrawn complaint or reverse a censure.

metadata.synopsis: TE John Hardie appealed his Metro Atlanta Presbytery conviction on three charges of breaking ordination vows and indefinite suspension, alleging seventeen procedural and evidentiary errors. Applying BCO 39-2/3 clear-error deference, the SJC denied every specification and upheld the judgment and censure. It found no clear error in the BCO 31-2 investigation, indictment/prosecutor process, commission membership, evidence rulings, scheduling, alleged prejudice, or censure. It assessed transcription costs equally while encouraging MAP to absorb them, and cautioned that an absent commissioner's vote might support a future challenge.

relationships.title: Thompson v. South Florida Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

metadata.synopsis: Chastain appealed Heritage Presbytery’s 2006 excommunication and deposition. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order because Chastain had renounced PCA jurisdiction on May 8, 2006. Consequently, Presbytery’s later proceedings were moot and SJC 2005-1 remained in effect. The SJC did not reach the merits. A concurrence questioned the discipline process after renunciation; a dissent argued the majority lacked constitutional authority to recognize unilateral withdrawal and thereby undercut discipline.

metadata.synopsis: An appeal challenged a presbytery's conviction of a minister for divisive behavior and its indefinite suspension from office and the sacraments. The SJC affirmed: the charge was lawful because publicly publishing disagreement with the session after it acted violated his ordination vows to subjection and peace/unity, even though “divisive” is not a constitutional term; the censure was not unjust absent repentance; procedural errors did not require reversal or remand. A dissent argued the charge failed BCO 29-1’s Scripture-proof requirement.

metadata.synopsis: A minister appealed three convictions and suspension that would automatically become indefinite absent repentance. The SJC sustained the appeal: unauthorized committee citations and admonition without process could not support guilt, and multiple trial violations were fatally prejudicial. It set aside the judgment, dismissed the citation and admonition charges, and revoked both censures. The inappropriate-language charge was not adjudicated on its merits; Presbytery could retry it on remand or dismiss it.

metadata.synopsis: A church member appealed convictions and excommunication arising from vulgar statements to two patients, challenging the lack of pretrial reconciliation, recusals, the prosecutor’s participation in deliberations, and Presbytery procedure. The SJC left guilt intact and denied a new trial, though it held that a prosecutor may not deliberate as a judge. It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. It remanded only to impose indefinite suspension from the Sacraments and conditions pending satisfactory evidence of repentance.
